result.plan_implied_asker: a fundamental long/short fund testing a substitution mechanism to size DraftKings positions
result.what_would_falsify: Flat event-time coefficients beta_0..beta_6 (no post-adoption divergence in DraftKings deposit dollars), placebo/negative-control outcomes moving, or partial-identification breakdown M below ~1 — any of these means abandon the substitution claim.

issues.summary: The single most decisive check — does adopting Kalshi coincide with any drop in DraftKings spend at all — is buried behind a week of taxonomy work plus a full matching and stacked-DiD build.
issues.why_it_applies_here: A crude raw event-time plot of DraftKings deposit dollars around first Kalshi debit for eligible adopters can be produced in a day and would tell you whether there is any visible level shift to explain. If adopters show zero movement, the entire matching/PML/partial-ID apparatus is wasted. The plan schedules the parallel-trends plot inside Validation, after all machinery is built.
issues.what_breaks: Weeks of taxonomy and matching effort are committed before the premise (any observable substitution) is confirmed to exist.
issues.fix: Run the unmatched adopter-vs-own-baseline event-time plot as step one, pre-registered as a go/no-go: no visible divergence in the raw series kills or pauses the build.

issues.summary: The plan does not test where substitution should be absent within the gambling category as a positive discriminator — its placebos are all non-gambling outcomes.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The mechanism is 'event contracts substitute for sportsbook wagering.' If Kalshi adoption reduces DraftKings AND FanDuel/BetMGM equally, that is category-wide gambling attrition (income shock, self-exclusion, life event), not Kalshi substitution. The FanDuel-only placebo pipeline tests the reverse, but held-out competitor spend among DraftKings adopters is used only as a balance covariate, not as an outcome that should move if substitution is real vs generic.
issues.what_breaks: A generic decline in all gambling spend gets attributed to Kalshi substitution, inflating the DraftKings-specific read.
issues.fix: Add competitor sportsbook spend (FanDuel/BetMGM/Caesars) as a co-outcome: substitution predicts DraftKings falls more than competitors among Kalshi adopters; parallel declines falsify the Kalshi-specific story.

issues.summary: No stated translation from panel deposit-dollar deltas to a DraftKings revenue/GGR impact, so the output cannot yet move position sizing as claimed.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Output is meant to change position sizing on DraftKings. A per-user deposit-dollar decline among Kalshi adopters is not a revenue impact without knowing Kalshi penetration of DraftKings' user base and the panel's representativeness of that base. The plan wisely avoids fabricating a number, but also never states the bridge needed to size the trade.
issues.what_breaks: The PM asks 'so how much does this move DraftKings revenue' and the study has no anchor; the result risks being over- or under-weighted in sizing.
issues.fix: Add a scoping step: estimate Kalshi adoption rate within the DraftKings-active panel and state explicitly that firm-level revenue impact = per-adopter effect x adoption share, flagged as the next deliverable rather than asserted.

result.overall: A genuinely strong, well-specified within-name causal design that fits the firm and the question, with a real falsifier, thoughtful placebos, and appropriate Type-I caution for a sizing decision. Two fixes matter: front-load the crude raw event-time check as a cheap go/no-go before building the matching apparatus, and add competitor-sportsbook spend as a co-outcome so Kalshi-specific substitution is distinguished from generic gambling attrition. The economics-to-sizing bridge is missing but is a next-step scoping gap, not a flaw in the causal work.

result.plan_implied_asker: a systematic panel-econometrics shop with an academic causal-inference bench
result.what_would_falsify: Permutation/mechanical null indistinguishable at 5%; placebos (grocery/streaming, non-legal states, neobank/P2P fake treatment) non-zero; six leads jointly significant; event-study ATT and regression β disagree beyond ~2x; out-of-sample 2024->2025 prediction fails.

issues.summary: The single cheapest test that could kill the whole idea — does Kalshi adoption coincide with a within-user DK drop at all — is buried behind an enormous estimation apparatus.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan's first usable output arrives only after descriptor dictionary, PPML/asinh models, IV construction, Callaway-Sant'Anna, and power calcs. But a simple binned event-study plot of mean net DK funding in months t-6..t+6 around first Kalshi use, on the non-brokerage legal-state subsample, would show in days whether any displacement exists. If that plot is flat, everything downstream is wasted.
issues.what_breaks: Weeks of analyst and engineer time are committed before the premise is shown to hold; a doomed idea takes months to kill instead of a week.
issues.fix: Front-load the raw within-user before/after mean plot with the mechanical-null overlay as step one, pre-committed as a gate: if no visible displacement survives the permuted null crudely, stop.

issues.summary: The methodological arsenal exceeds what a 30-person fundamental L/S PM can evaluate or defend, and much of it is redundant.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Driscoll-Kraay, wild bootstrap, ppmlhdfe, asinh, Arellano-Bond, IV with Kleibergen-Paap, Callaway-Sant'Anna, randomization inference — this is a publication-grade stack for a firm whose output is position sizing on named companies. The PM will ask 'what would have to be true for it to be wrong,' not whether the KP F-stat cleared 20. Most of these estimators answer the same question; three of them (donut event study, permutation null, placebos) carry the decision.
issues.what_breaks: The result becomes hard to defend internally precisely because no one on the desk can independently verify the machinery; researcher degrees of freedom multiply across a dozen specifications.
issues.fix: Lead with the within-user event study plus placebo panel — both directly inspectable — and relegate IV/Arellano-Bond to 'only if the simple result is marginal.' State which specifications are decision-relevant vs. robustness color.

issues.summary: The denominator/simultaneity problem is real and the plan's own primary regressor may not escape it.
issues.why_it_applies_here: H1's regressor is Kalshi share K/(K+DK+FD), which mechanically contains DK on both sides; a fall in DK raises share even with no behavioral substitution. The plan knows this (baseline-deflated K/W̄, permuted null) — but W̄ is a fixed pre-period mean, so a user whose total wallet shrinks for unrelated reasons still shows rising K/W̄ while DK falls. The permutation test guards mechanical reshuffling, not common wallet-shrinkage shocks.
issues.what_breaks: A significant β could reflect users cutting all discretionary spend (of which both Kalshi-funding and DK are part) rather than Kalshi displacing DK.
issues.fix: Lean on the wallet-accounting decomposition (does savings/discretionary rise as DK falls?) and the FD-symmetry contrast as the primary economic identification, not the share regression; treat the K/W̄ coefficient as corroborating.

issues.summary: Deposit-to-revenue conversion for DraftKings is asserted via take rates but the link to the equity thesis — what a displacement number means for DKNG earnings — is never built.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The panel covers a sliver of DK's user base; '$X displaced per 10-point share rise' on the panel does not extrapolate to a firmwide revenue delta without a panel-coverage/representativeness step the plan omits. The headline dollar figure risks being scaled into an implied DKNG revenue hit that the data cannot support.
issues.what_breaks: A PM could anchor position sizing on a panel-local number mistaken for a firmwide effect.
issues.fix: Add an explicit step estimating panel coverage as a share of DK's deposit base and state that the deliverable is the sign, magnitude-per-user, and concentration in high-value users — not a firmwide revenue forecast — unless coverage is validated.

issues.summary: The plan is largely a fixed pipeline; it states kill criteria but not which branches drop when.
issues.why_it_applies_here: It pre-commits pass/fail thresholds (good) but runs pooled-plus-ten-splits, IV, event study and Arellano-Bond regardless of whether the headline effect is obvious or null. If the raw event study shows a clean strong effect, the IV and dynamic-panel work are unnecessary; if it shows nothing, the cuts are pointless.
issues.what_breaks: Effort is spent symmetrically across a decision tree that early results should prune.
issues.fix: Add explicit branching: 'if event study + placebos pass cleanly and effect is large, skip IV; if marginal, run IV; if null on the gate, stop.'

result.overall: The econometrics is genuinely strong — the mechanical-null, placebo battery, wallet-accounting, and out-of-sample gate are exactly the right falsifiers, and the plan takes the denominator and attribution problems seriously. The two real problems are ordering and calibration: the single cheap test that could kill the idea is buried behind a research-grade estimation stack that this fundamental desk cannot fully evaluate or defend, and the pipeline runs symmetrically rather than pruning on early results. Reorder to front-load the raw within-user event study plus placebos as a gate, designate three decision-relevant tests versus robustness color, and ensure the deliverable stays at 'sign, per-user magnitude, and concentration in high-value users' rather than a firmwide revenue number the panel coverage cannot yet support.

result.plan_implied_asker: a fundamental L/S fund with an alt-data panel team and 6-18 month horizon
result.what_would_falsify: Refit on excluded consumption-priced names; equal performance sinks the thesis. Also: MAU fails to beat two-way FE benchmark C out-of-sample under Diebold-Mariano p<0.05.

issues.summary: The deliverable predicts ARR (the fundamental), but the fund trades named stocks on a 6-18mo horizon, and the plan never tests whether the MAU-to-ARR signal is incremental to consensus at print.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The output is meant to change position sizing on named companies. Predicting ARR accurately is worthless if consensus already prices it — and the plan captures Visible Alpha consensus but only uses it as a dispersion yardstick, never as the thing to beat. The benchmark set (carry-forward, trailing growth, FE-without-MAU) is mechanical, not the market. Getting ARR right and the stock not moving is the exact failure mode this fund's PM will ask about.
issues.what_breaks: The validation step declares victory when MAU beats naive extrapolation C, but a signal can beat C and still be fully priced by sell-side. The 'edge' is asserted as better measurement but never diffed against consensus expectations.
issues.fix: Add a step: does the MAU-implied ARR surprise predict the actual ARR surprise versus Visible Alpha consensus, and does the residual predict post-print stock returns over the trading horizon? That is the investable question. Beating C is table stakes, not the deliverable.

issues.summary: The falsifier (refit on consumption-priced names) is a good negative control but is scheduled at the very end, behind the entire estimation and validation apparatus.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The consumption-names control is cheap and could invalidate the mechanism story early — if MAU 'predicts' revenue equally well for Snowflake, the signal is measuring something generic (size, growth momentum) not seat billing. Running it last means the expensive machinery is built before the premise is stress-tested.
issues.what_breaks: Weeks of panel construction and econometrics are sunk before the one test that could show the mechanism is illusory. Front-loading it would prune a doomed branch cheaply.
issues.fix: Move the consumption-names negative control forward: fit the simple within-company log-log regression on both seat and consumption names first. If MAU tracks revenue equally in both, stop.

issues.summary: MAU is an unvalidated proxy for seats; the mechanism requires MAU-per-seat and price-per-seat to drift slowly, but the plan asserts this rather than measuring it.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Named companies disclose seat/customer counts and net revenue retention. The plan controls for price drift via Wayback snapshots but never checks the core link: does MAU actually move with billed seats within a company, or with engagement per seat (which is decorrelated from billing)? Shelfware — paid seats not logging in — is exactly the case where MAU and ARR diverge, and it is handled only as an asymmetry interaction after the fact.
issues.what_breaks: If MAU-per-seat is not slow-moving, β is unstable and the whole 1%-MAU-implies-β%-ARR framing is measuring engagement, not billing. The signal would work in expansion and fail in the flat/decline regimes that matter most for shorts.
issues.fix: Where disclosed, regress MAU on reported seats/customers directly for a subset of names to validate the proxy-to-target link before assuming it. Report the MAU/seat ratio time series.

issues.summary: ~40 effective clusters and 35-60 names with heterogeneous business models is thin for the pooled panel econometrics stacked on top.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan itself flags ~40 effective clusters, then applies CIPS, Westerlund, ECM, Driscoll-Kraay, wild cluster bootstrap, Pesaran CD. Wild cluster bootstrap and CD tests are near their reliability floor at 40 clusters. The real evidence here is within-name consistency over quarters, which the rolling-origin and LOCO checks capture well — the panel-cointegration layer adds researcher degrees of freedom without adding conviction the PM can use.
issues.what_breaks: The sophisticated panel tests will produce numbers that look authoritative but are underpowered at this N, and the PM cannot defend them. The credible evidence is the per-name trend-tracking, which the simpler benchmarks and rolling-origin already deliver.
issues.fix: Lead with the simple within-name check and rolling-origin MAPE; keep the panel unit-root/cointegration battery as an appendix robustness note, not a gate. The corroborating simple check the audience can verify is already present — make it the headline.

result.overall: This is a well-constructed, genuinely rigorous plan that correctly matches the firm's horizon, infrastructure and defensibility needs, and it engages falsification seriously with a real negative control. The blocking gap is target substitution: it predicts ARR accurately but never tests whether that prediction is incremental to sell-side consensus or translates into stock moves the fund can trade — beating a naive carry-forward is not the same as an edge. Fix by making the consensus-surprise-to-return link the deliverable, validate MAU-against-disclosed-seats before assuming the proxy, and move the cheap consumption-names control to the front.

result.plan_implied_asker: a fundamental L/S fund with an alt-data panel team wanting a defensible nowcast across a small set of seat-based SaaS names
result.what_would_falsify: Gate failure: β̂ not positive/significant at 5% under block bootstrap, or β̂ outside [0.5,1.5], or within-company partial correlation <0.45, or unstable across halves/leave-one-out — any of which yields a documented negative result rather than a fallback.

issues.summary: The deliverable nowcasts ARR growth, but the fund's output is position sizing — and the plan never connects the ARR nowcast to stock outperformance or to what consensus already expects.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The firm sizes named positions on a 6–18mo horizon; being right about ARR is only investable if the ARR view differs from what is already priced. The plan's only nod to consensus is a surprise-space regression at the end (model-minus-consensus), which is the right instinct but is buried as a validation add-on, not the gating question. A perfectly calibrated seat nowcast that agrees with sell-side estimates changes no position.
issues.what_breaks: Even a fully passing gate and nowcast could produce zero edge if the panel MAU signal is already embedded in consensus (these are heavily-covered names with the same alt-data vendors sold to everyone). The whole pipeline can succeed on its own terms and still not move sizing.
issues.fix: Promote the model-minus-consensus surprise test to a co-primary gate: does the MAU-derived ARR nowcast systematically anticipate consensus revisions and, ideally, post-print drift on these names? Kill early if the signal is coincident with, not ahead of, consensus.

issues.summary: Panel MAU on authenticated post-login paths is a weak proxy for billable seats precisely where the money is — enterprise SaaS with managed devices, SSO, VPN and desktop clients.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan's own pitfalls list 'enterprise blindness' as the dominant failure mode, then relegates it to a coverage-trend warning and a second vendor. For Atlassian, Smartsheet, monday, the seats that matter most are exactly the ones panels see least (corporate networks, thick clients). Coverage isn't just noisy — it is systematically biased against the highest-value cohort, and that bias can trend with product/deployment mix.
issues.what_breaks: The gate regression β could pass on the visible slice while the invisible slice drives actual ARR growth, giving a signal that works in backtest on disclosers and fails on the names you'd actually trade. The coverage-drift kill (>10%/yr) may not catch a stable-but-biased coverage floor.
issues.fix: Make coverage adequacy a first, cheap gate before any modeling: for the seat-like disclosers, plot panel-MAU/disclosed-seats level and its stability per company. If coverage is <~a few percent or the level is unstable for the enterprise names, kill those names up front rather than modeling them.

issues.summary: Contemporaneous nowcasting of a quantity most companies disclose within weeks offers little on a 6–18 month horizon.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The primary claim is a contemporaneous proxy; the nowcast fires five business days after quarter end. The fund holds 6–18 months. A nowcast of a number reported ~4–6 weeks later is only valuable if it (a) beats consensus ahead of the print or (b) predicts the trajectory several quarters out. The lead-quarter diagnostic is the valuable piece and is treated as secondary ('a lead becomes the nowcast core' only if it appears).
issues.what_breaks: If the signal is only contemporaneous and not leading, the informational value decays to near zero for this horizon — you learn the ARR growth a few weeks before it's disclosed, which rarely justifies a sizing change held for a year.
issues.fix: Elevate the leading-indicator test to primary. Gate on whether MAU growth predicts ARR growth one-to-two quarters ahead, not just contemporaneously; a contemporaneous-only result should be treated as a marginal outcome, not success.

issues.summary: The sample is a handful of seat-disclosing names, several of which are not the names to be traded, and cross-sectional generalization is thin.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The gate is validated on seat-like disclosers (ADP, Paycom, Dayforce, Dropbox, etc.), but the tradable universe is the seat-based SaaS names that don't cleanly disclose seats — that is the whole point of building the proxy. Success on disclosers is the correct calibration approach, but the plan should be explicit that it is generalizing from where seats ARE disclosed to where they are NOT, and that this leap is untested.
issues.what_breaks: β estimated on ADP/Paycom (payroll, near-perfect seat visibility) may not transfer to Asana/monday (fuzzy free tiers, deskless users). The two-thirds-of-firms consistency check partly guards this but pooling heterogeneous business models risks a mechanical average that fits no single tradable name.
issues.fix: State the generalization explicitly and add a per-company consistency-over-time judgement for the actual target names, rather than leaning on pooled significance. Treat the disclosers as a training/validation set and the target names as held-out, judged on trend agreement where any partial disclosure exists.

issues.summary: Ridge + nested CV + empirical-Bayes shrinkage is more machinery than the small-N problem needs and harder to defend to the PM.
issues.why_it_applies_here: With a dozen-ish companies and a lagged-dependent-variable nowcast, the simple pooled FE regression plus damped AR(1) baseline already resolves most of the question. The ridge/EB layer adds researcher degrees of freedom the pitfalls section then has to police (specification count). The plan does pair it with a simple baseline, which mitigates — but the marginal value over a shrunk pooled OLS is unlikely to survive OOS on N this small.
issues.what_breaks: Extra tuning surface invites overfit on tiny folds and gives the PM a harder-to-explain model without materially better forecasts.
issues.fix: Run the simple pooled FE + damped-AR(1) nowcast first as the deliverable; only add ridge/EB if the simple version demonstrably underperforms on walk-forward, and report the delta.

result.overall: Methodologically careful, well-firm-fit, and unusually good at pre-committing kill criteria and falsifiers — this is a competent proxy-calibration plan. But it answers the wrong end of the question for this fund: it nowcasts ARR growth without establishing that the ARR view is (a) ahead of consensus and (b) tradable on a 6–18mo horizon, and it under-weights that panel coverage is structurally blind to exactly the enterprise seats that drive ARR. Promote the consensus-surprise and leading-indicator tests to primary gates, front-load a cheap coverage-adequacy screen, and trim the ridge/EB layer until the simple version fails.

result.plan_implied_asker: an alt-data L/S fund needing a defensible ID-to-ticker matching layer before it can trade the panel
result.what_would_falsify: Null (permuted-customer) silhouette unbeaten, bootstrap Jaccard <0.6, or cross-window ARI <0.4 — any of these forces reporting only country/business-model separation and refusing named matches.

issues.summary: The plan runs the full clustering/naming/validation pipeline before establishing whether any named match can be verified against ground truth the desk trusts.
issues.why_it_applies_here: What kills the work is a confident wrong match. The entire validation ladder tests internal cohesion and stability (silhouette, Jaccard, ARI, permutation null) — none of which establishes correctness of a name. A cluster can be sharply separated, stable, and beat the null while being mapped to the wrong bank, because the Hungarian assignment rests on rank-agreement between panel-customer counts and market share, which is a plausibility heuristic, not a verification.
issues.what_breaks: The 'named institution' tier (B/C) is the only output the desk can trade on, and it arrives at the very end resting on an unverified assumption. The PM's question — what would have to be true for this to be wrong — is not answered by any stated step, because no independent external check of a name is ever performed.
issues.fix: Front-load a ground-truth anchor set: identify a handful of IDs whose bank is knowable with near-certainty from an external tell (a bank-specific domestic scheme monopoly, a unique product, a regulatory quirk, a merchant/counterparty ID that only one institution issues) and confirm the pipeline recovers them before building the rest. If even a handful cannot be independently confirmed, the naming tier is undeliverable and the project stops at archetype.

issues.summary: The named-match decision rule (rank agreement plus a margin) has no stated false-match rate and no external calibration of what the margin buys.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Given Type I dominance here — a wrong name means sizing on another bank's customers — the naming gate needs a quantified error rate, not a 'preset margin' and '≤3 candidates.' The plan never says how often the constrained-assignment step would name the wrong institution when tested against known cases, so the PM cannot judge whether Tier B is safe to trade.
issues.what_breaks: Constrained-assignment naming step: the accept threshold is asserted, not calibrated. Downstream, the desk cannot distinguish a defensible named match from a lucky rank coincidence in a concentrated country-archetype cell where two banks have similar share.
issues.fix: Using the anchor set above, measure the empirical wrong-name rate of the assignment rule at candidate margins and set the accept threshold to a false-match rate the desk pre-commits to (e.g. name only when demonstrably below X%). Report the confusion cases.

issues.summary: The plan is over-scoped for what is, at core, a matching-feasibility question that could be triaged far more cheaply.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Three clustering algorithms, co-association reconciliation, NMF co-holding loadings, PageRank, GMM full-covariance, UMAP, and a 500-iteration Hennig bootstrap are all committed up front. But the binding question — can an anonymized ID be tied to a specific bank with acceptable error — may be answerable for the easy cases (country-monopoly domestic schemes, unique counterparty IDs, dominant incumbents) with simple deterministic tells, and impossible for the hard cases regardless of clustering sophistication. The 3-person data team and one engineer can operate this, but much of it may be wasted motion.
issues.what_breaks: Weeks of pipeline construction precede any evidence that named matching is achievable, committing analyst time before the cheap version has shown the idea works.
issues.fix: First pass: attempt deterministic identification via unique institutional tells (scheme issuance, unique counterparty/BIN signatures, single-bank products) on the highest-share IDs. This alone may resolve the tradeable names. Reserve the clustering machinery for the residual and for archetype-only tiers where deterministic tells fail.

issues.summary: Country/archetype separation is confirmatory of what is already knowable, not incremental — only the named tier is potentially investable.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The desk wants to underwrite specific listed banks. Knowing an ID is 'a German savings-specialist' is not attachable to a ticker and adds nothing over public market-structure data. The edge exists only if the named tier clears, so the plan's value is entirely contingent on the naming step the validation does not verify.
issues.what_breaks: If naming fails, the deliverable collapses to a restatement of ECB/EBA market structure the fund already has, with no tradeable output despite full pipeline cost.
issues.fix: State explicitly that archetype-only is a negative result for this fund's purpose, and gate continued spend on the naming feasibility check succeeding first.

result.overall: This is a technically strong, self-aware capability build — the pitfalls section anticipates account-role confounding, panel skew, and aggregator/white-label IDs, and the negative-result path is honestly pre-committed. But it is misordered for the one thing that kills the work: the entire validation ladder proves cohesion and stability, never correctness of a name, and the confident-wrong-match risk lives entirely in an uncalibrated rank-assignment rule that arrives last. Before building the pipeline, establish an external ground-truth anchor set and measure the false-name rate of the assignment rule; if a handful of names cannot be independently confirmed cheaply, the tradeable tier is undeliverable and that should be established in week one, not month three.

result.plan_implied_asker: an alt-data-mature systematic-leaning L/S fund that treats a confident wrong match as the killing risk
result.what_would_falsify: Below 40% of panel deposit volume assignable at \u226595% precision on held-out institutions a country is declared not identifiable; permuted fingerprints must score at chance and phantom IDs must abstain.

issues.summary: The matching machinery (min-cost flow, Jonker\u2013Volgenant, Sinkhorn marginals, Venn\u2013Abers/split-conformal, Wasserstein/JS scoring) is not defensible to the PM who must ask 'what would have to be true for this to be wrong.'
issues.why_it_applies_here: The stated use case requires each accepted bank\u2192ID match to be defensible to an investment committee before a position is sized; the killing risk is a confident wrong match. An optimal-transport assignment with conformal calibration cannot be traced by hand \u2014 the PM cannot see why ID 4471 was called ING rather than ABN. The plan owes a simple corroborating check the audience can verify itself and does not provide one.
issues.what_breaks: Every accepted match feeds a position, but the acceptance is a black box; the PM cannot underwrite the one thing that kills the desk.
issues.fix: For each accepted match, produce a one-page human-readable dossier: the 2-3 features that dominated the score (e.g. Kindergeld-digit signature, NUTS-3 branch overlap, salary payday concentration), shown as raw distributions against the anchor, plus the runner-up candidate and why it lost. The optimal-transport layer can run underneath, but a person must be able to confirm the top matches by eye.

issues.summary: The joint-assignment global optimizer is complexity ahead of demonstrated need; a simple per-ID scoring pass should be shown to fail before the transport layer is built.
issues.why_it_applies_here: In concentrated markets (NL, SE) with a handful of large banks, most IDs will separate on n_share and geography alone \u2014 the injective-map hypothesis says exactly this. The min-cost-flow-with-capacities apparatus only earns its place in fragmented markets (350 Sparkassen) where the plan itself predicts identification fails. So the heavy machinery is being built precisely where the answer is 'not identifiable.'
issues.what_breaks: Engineer and data-team weeks go into Sinkhorn/Gibbs entropy matching before anyone has shown a naive greedy assignment is insufficient in the markets that matter.
issues.fix: Run the Netherlands pilot with plain per-ID likelihood scoring and greedy assignment first. Add the joint optimizer only if greedy produces mutually inconsistent assignments at the target precision.

issues.summary: Validation-label supply (25-60 per country, floor 15) is thin, and precision at the \u226595% target is being certified on very few positives.
issues.why_it_applies_here: To claim \u226595% precision you need enough validated true matches that a handful of errors moves the estimate materially; with 25-60 labels per country and leave-one-institution-out refitting, the precision confidence interval will be wide. The plan is honest that below 15 it is unvalidatable, but 25-60 still cannot distinguish 95% from 85% precision reliably.
issues.what_breaks: A country could pass the 40%/95% gate on a precision estimate that is really a small-sample fluke, and the desk sizes on it.
issues.fix: Report precision with its Clopper-Pearson interval and require the lower bound (not point estimate) to clear 95%; expand consented-survey seeding where the label count is marginal, or restrict deployment to institutions with direct provider-revealed seeds.

issues.summary: The largest concrete deliverable is a boolean identifiability map, but the firm's actual downstream need \u2014 which specific tickers can be underwritten \u2014 is only implicit.
issues.why_it_applies_here: This is a capability build and correctly scoped as one; success is measurement, not a P&L. But the firm names four behaviors (deposit flows, salary capture, acquisition, attrition) it wants to underwrite. The plan should state which of those signals survive the match uncertainty \u2014 a 92%-precision match may be fine for a directional attrition read but unsafe for a levered pairs trade.
issues.what_breaks: A binary 'identifiable' verdict hands the desk matches without telling them which use each match is good enough for.
issues.fix: Deliver, per accepted match, the confidence and the customer-count support alongside a note on which of the four underwriting signals that support can carry, so the PM sizes accordingly.

result.overall: This is a well-constructed capability build with the right error posture \u2014 Type-I-dominant, abstain-heavy, kill criterion and negative controls front-loaded, register separation to prevent anchor leakage, and genuine engagement with what would make it wrong. The binding defect is that the matching method is too sophisticated for the PM who must defend each match; optimal transport and conformal calibration cannot answer 'what would have to be true for this to be wrong' unless each accepted match ships with a hand-checkable dossier. Start with the Netherlands using plain per-ID scoring, and build the transport layer only if the simple version demonstrably fails.

result.plan_implied_asker: single-name event-driven catalyst desk reading a specific corporate structuring event
result.what_would_falsify: A signing-document condition met on schedule (H0-a); a subsidiary/keepwell/ECL substitution (observation wrong); withdrawals across unrelated vehicles (treasury policy); deconsolidation entry with VIE footnote change and CFO commentary (H0-b); no independent second-source qualification within twelve months and no available advanced packaging (H1 lacks mechanism); a take-or-pay/volume floor/RVG replacing the guarantee (risk transfer falsified).

issues.summary: The comparable-release coding exercise (40-60 cases across three strata) is a generalizable base-rate study bolted onto a single-name call and largely duplicates work the document read already does.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The desk has two analysts, no dataset-building capacity, and the question is whether THIS situation is mispriced now. The signing documents themselves state whether the release was a scheduled condition (H0-a) — reading the Guaranty Release Date and completion triggers resolves the dominant benign explanation directly, without coding 50 unrelated project-finance deals. The base-rate prior is useful as a sanity anchor but the plan front-loads a weeks-long coding project the staff cannot cheaply run.
issues.what_breaks: Methodology step consumes the scarce analyst weeks before the catalyst window closes; a weeks-to-months horizon can pass while comparables are being coded.
issues.fix: Read the original documents first — if the release is a scheduled condition met on terms, stop. Only if the trigger is negotiated/unexplained does the comparable set add value, and then cap it at a handful of genuine semiconductor-capacity JV analogs, not 50 cross-strata deals.

issues.summary: The ~25x likelihood-ratio hurdle against a 20:1-30:1 prior is a manufactured quantitative bar the evidence sources cannot actually feed.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The H1 evidence is qualitative and sparse — hiring reqs, MPW activity, teardowns, customs data on one situation. There is no way to compute a calibrated 25x likelihood ratio from these; the number invents precision the design cannot deliver and risks either false rigor or an impossible-to-clear gate that discards a real signal (Type II) or a rationalized clearing of it (Type I).
issues.what_breaks: The Bayesian framing implies a numeric verdict that the actual evidence stream cannot support, letting the analyst assign convenient LRs to reach a predetermined conclusion.
issues.fix: Keep the directional prior (benign causes dominate, demand strong contemporaneous second-source evidence) but drop the pseudo-numeric LR. State the qualitative pattern that would count as confirmation and the pattern that would count as kill — the falsifier list already does this well.

issues.summary: H3 (souring project) is flagged as externally identical to H1 but the separation rests entirely on demand-side evidence that may not be observable in the window.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan correctly notes H3 and H1 have opposite trade implications and identical financing footprints. But the demand-side signals it relies on to separate them (node slip, insourcing, demand shortfall) are exactly the things a hyperscaler and foundry disclose last and least. If separation fails, the trade direction is undetermined.
issues.what_breaks: Even a clean H1-vs-H0 result leaves the position exposed to being long the wrong sign if the release actually reflects a souring project.
issues.fix: Make H1/H3 separation a pre-committed gate: if demand-side evidence cannot distinguish them within the catalyst window, the situation is not tradeable and the position should not be put on regardless of how strong the strategic read looks.

result.overall: A genuinely strong single-name plan that fits the desk: document-first, catalyst-horizoned, with real pre-registered falsifiers and explicit engagement with the benign alternatives and the opposite-sign H3 case. The main defects are self-imposed over-engineering — a 50-case comparable-coding study and a pseudo-numeric likelihood-ratio hurdle that neither the staff nor the evidence can support — which should be trimmed in favor of reading the signing documents first, since a scheduled-condition release kills the thesis in days. Watch that H1 and H3 remain separable within the window; if not, the situation is not tradeable.

result.plan_implied_asker: single-name event-driven credit/equity desk trading a catalyst over weeks-to-months
result.what_would_falsify: Release language verbatim as-signed with the pre-agreed test (COD/DSCR) met; no consent solicitation or consent fee; VIE exposure-to-loss dropping below released notional; capacity volumes flat or rising; no second-source qualification predating the change. Any two of these and H1 is rejected.

issues.summary: The near-dispositive H3 test relies on back-solving redacted contract quantities and on a QoQ delta in the hyperscaler's VIE maximum-exposure-to-loss disclosure that may not be granular or timely enough to attribute to this SPV.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan itself names the exposure-to-loss delta as 'best H3 test' but hyperscalers disclose VIE max-exposure in aggregate, not per-SPV; a single new SPV can be swamped by other VIEs and the disclosure lags by a quarter. Back-solving redactions under 601(b)(10)(iv) is explicitly flagged as necessary because the key numbers are hidden.
issues.what_breaks: The H3 kill/confirm step may return an unmeasurable or ambiguous number, leaving the H1-vs-H3 distinction unresolved right where the plan says it is decided.
issues.fix: State a fallback when the aggregate delta is uninformative: rely on the as-signed guarantee article language and reserve/LC face directly, and mark H3 'indeterminate' rather than forcing a read from a noisy aggregate.

issues.summary: Qualification-timing evidence (second source predating the change) is inferred from noisy public tells — job postings, conference papers, bill-of-lading, EDA/IP disclosures — none of which timestamp a decision cleanly.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The H1 story hinges on qualification preceding the guarantor removal by 18-36 months, but the listed corroborants are lagging and ambiguous: a PDK license or IEDM paper signals engagement, not committed second-sourcing on this design family, and dates are fuzzy.
issues.what_breaks: 'No qualification predating the change' is one of the named killers; if the timing evidence is inherently soft, that killer can be neither cleanly triggered nor cleanly cleared, weakening the falsification test.
issues.fix: Require at least one hard, dated corroborant (a mask-set/tape-out order, a dated NRE payment, a specific packaging requal booking) before treating pre-dating qualification as established; treat soft tells as supporting-only.

issues.summary: The document-heavy front end is a large fixed workload before the cheapest disconfirming check.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan does place 'check the price reaction first' in pitfalls and orders H2/H3 before H1, but the 300-page as-signed document pull and redaction back-solve is heavy and could be gated behind a first-pass read of whether the release simply matches vintage-standard COD/DSCR language.
issues.what_breaks: Analyst time is the binding constraint on a two-analyst desk; if the release is boilerplate springing off a met test (H2), most of the supply-agreement and channel work is wasted.
issues.fix: Explicitly front the single check that most cheaply kills the thesis: does the release language match the pre-agreed COD/DSCR test in the as-signed docs and was that test met? If yes, stop before the supply-agreement and channel program.

result.overall: A well-constructed single-name event-driven plan that fits the desk exactly: legal-document primary work, expert channel, fast kill criteria, cheapest-disconfirmation-first ordering, an explicit falsifier, a base-rate cross-check, and sizing anchored to observable release spread rather than an invented alpha figure. It correctly predicts the target (is this situation mispriced now) and matches the Type-I-dominant, IC-traceable posture of a concentrated catalyst book. The real weaknesses are measurement, not design — the two near-dispositive tests (VIE exposure-to-loss delta and qualification-timing) rest on disclosures that may be too aggregated or too soft to trigger the stated killers cleanly, so the plan should name fallbacks and demand at least one hard dated corroborant before committing capital.

result.plan_implied_asker: a large systematic equity firm with production ML, tick data and a replicating research committee, days-to-weeks horizon
result.what_would_falsify: Null pre-registered: peer-relative tone residual adds no risk-adjusted return beyond SUE, announcement return, momentum and style factors; net alpha below 30bp break-even is declared a paper result; a clean null is treated as a real output.

issues.summary: The kill test — does any tone measure survive costs and orthogonalization — sits at the very end behind a full custom NLP model build.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan front-loads ~1.5-2B-token domain-adaptive MLM pretraining, a 6k-sentence gold annotation effort and 150k silver labels before ever checking whether a cheap tone proxy (Loughran-McDonald, off-the-shelf FinBERT) produces a residual signal that survives the FF5+MOM/SUE controls and 30bp break-even. LM and FinBERT are named only as benchmarks-to-beat, not as a first-pass gate.
issues.what_breaks: Weeks of GPU pretraining and annotation are sunk before the premise — that peer-relative call tone carries priced-in-days-to-weeks information beyond PEAD — is shown to hold at all. If LM tone already dies against the announcement-return control, the entire custom encoder was wasted.
issues.fix: Run the whole pipeline first with LM and stock FinBERT tone as the signal. Only if a crude tone residual shows net-of-cost promise does the DeBERTa domain-adaptation and gold-annotation build earn its place. Make this an explicit pre-committed gate.

issues.summary: No inspectable intermediate output is scheduled before the modelling commitment; human review appears only as post-hoc audits.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan lists a 200-call EDGAR timestamp audit and coverage-by-decile tables, but these are framed as pitfall checks rather than early gates. The distribution of the tone measure, hand-traced Q&A reconstruction on sample calls, and coverage/missingness by year are the things that would catch a broken parser or imputed-timestamp contamination — and nothing forces them before the encoder is built.
issues.what_breaks: A systematic parsing error (e.g. operator boilerplate leaking, mislabeled Q&A vs prepared sections) propagates silently into H2, which is the most novel claim, and is only discoverable after full training.
issues.fix: Move timestamp audit, Q&A-pair spot checks and coverage tables to the front as a pass/fail data-integrity gate before any label or model work.

issues.summary: Timestamp imputation for calls lacking minute-level start uses the 8-K press-release time, which can precede the call and create look-ahead in the announcement-return control.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan flags imputed timestamps but still uses (−1,+1) announcement return and t+1 entry keyed off call time. For calls where the 8-K timestamp is the release not the call, the (−1,+1) window and the tone-availability assumption misalign — tone is not actually knowable at the entry point claimed.
issues.what_breaks: Portfolio entry at t+1 close assumes tone was observable; if the true call time is later than the imputed 8-K time, the signal is partly forward-looking and inflates alpha.
issues.fix: Exclude imputed-timestamp calls from the headline specification (keep as a robustness cut), or enforce entry strictly after a conservatively latest possible call time. The 200-call audit should quantify the imputation error distribution before deciding.

result.overall: Methodologically this is among the more disciplined systematic plans one could review: pre-registered primary spec, held-out 2023-2024 touched once, explicit break-even and capacity, negative controls, placebo, a real pre-committed null, and appropriate Type-II-leaning posture for a diversified quant book. The sophisticated NLP is corroborated by LM/FinBERT benchmarks and the committee can re-run it. The one real defect is sequencing and cost: the cheap tone proxies are demoted to benchmarks when they should be the first-pass kill test, so a large annotation-and-pretraining spend is committed before the premise is shown to survive PEAD controls and transaction costs. Reorder to gate on the crude version first and the plan is sound.

result.plan_implied_asker: a large systematic quant firm with tick data, production ML, and a replicating research committee
result.what_would_falsify: Tone t below 2.5 (2.9 Bonferroni), net spread under 3% annualised or IR under 0.4, wrong sign in more than 3 of 10 years, or spread concentrated in the bottom size quintile; plus placebo over [-63,-3] showing an incremental coefficient and vendor rank correlation above 0.7 indicating commodity duplication.

issues.summary: Vendor availability is used as the crowding proxy but the plan never diffs the final signal against what the vendor scores would already have captured beyond the one-month rank-correlation trial.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Edge here is whether the in-house tone signal is incremental to what is already sold and in books. The 0.7 rank-correlation trial checks duplication of construction, but two signals can correlate below 0.7 and still both be arbitraged. The plan infers crowding from seat cost and client count, which is a reasonable proxy, but does not test whether the net spread survives after orthogonalizing to the vendor score rather than merely using it as a control.
issues.what_breaks: Day 10 spread and Day 11-14 scope decision could greenlight a signal that is a slightly-decorrelated repackaging of a widely-licensed score, failing on capacity/crowding in production.
issues.fix: Add an explicit step regressing the in-house signal's returns on the licensed vendor score's returns and require the residual to retain a material fraction of the net spread before scope-out.

issues.summary: The 2004-2010 replication requiring t near 3 uses a period with materially different transcript coverage and market microstructure than the 2015+ primary sample.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Capital IQ / WRDS transcript coverage and timestamp reliability are thinner and less point-in-time in 2004-2010 than post-2015; the same LM within-firm-change construction may behave differently because the peer universe and coverage bias shift. Requiring t near 3 in a noisier, less-covered era could either falsely kill a real recent effect or falsely validate on a smaller, size-skewed early sample.
issues.what_breaks: Days 6-7 replication gate may reject or accept for reasons of data regime rather than signal decay, contaminating the decay-curve estimate that the whole prior rests on.
issues.fix: Report coverage and timestamp-quality diagnostics for 2004-2010 alongside the replication, and treat the early-period t as directional evidence for the decay curve rather than a hard second gate.

result.overall: A strong, well-sequenced plan that matches the firm and the blind-fit/OOS goal, front-loads a pre-registered kill gate, and correctly treats Type II asymmetry with judgeable thresholds and negative controls. It measures the target (peer-relative return, incremental to surprise/CAR/guidance) rather than a proxy, engages decay and crowding directly, and states real falsifiers. The two open items — proving incrementality to the licensed vendor score beyond a correlation trial, and treating the early-period replication as regime-sensitive — are secondary and do not block execution.

result.plan_implied_asker: a systematic quant equity shop with a full factor stack and pre-registration discipline
result.what_would_falsify: First-stage pooled announcement β<20bp/100bp or t<5 kills the premise; placebo/randomization must produce vanishing coefficients; split-sample 2015-2025 tested once; stability declared only if VR>=2 and bootstrap p<0.05.

issues.summary: The analytical machinery (Bai-Perron sup-F, Kalman β path, stationary block bootstrap, 2SLS, two-stage DCF for β*) is far beyond what this fund's PM and IC can evaluate or defend.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Output must 'be defensible to a PM who will ask what would have to be true for it to be wrong.' A Kalman-filtered time-varying β and a sup-F break test are not checkable by a fundamental IC; they cannot carry a sizing decision at a 30-person L/S shop with one engineer and no production ML.
issues.what_breaks: The estimation and stability sections produce numbers no one on the receiving end can interrogate, so the result either gets rubber-stamped or ignored — neither is a decision.
issues.fix: Lead with a simple, inspectable version: monthly Fama-MacBeth β with a plot of β by regime bucket and the raw scatter of ΔCAGR vs Δln(EV/EBITDA). Keep the sophisticated machinery as an appendix corroboration, not the primary deliverable.

issues.summary: The plan is scoped as a 22-year multi-regime econometric study when the fund needs a usable position-sizing input over a 6-18 month horizon.
issues.why_it_applies_here: H1 (regime-dependent β) and H2 (efficiency/drift) answer academic questions about market structure. The fund's actual use is: when a peer-relative revision hits, does the multiple re-rate in a direction and magnitude I can trade over 6-18 months? That is H2's underreaction leg plus a single stable β estimate — most of H1's regime apparatus is not decision-relevant.
issues.what_breaks: Analyst-months are spent on Bai-Perron breaks and Kalman paths that don't change a sizing rule, delaying the one output (does re-rating drift persist and is it tradeable) that the desk can act on.
issues.fix: Demote H1 to a robustness note. Make the drift/underreaction test (H2i) the primary deliverable, since that is the only leg producing an actionable, horizon-matched signal.

issues.summary: No explicit statement of what consensus/sell-side already believes about revision-to-rerating, so the incremental edge is asserted rather than established.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Post-earnings-drift and analyst-revision momentum are among the most documented and crowded anomalies in equity markets. The plan tests whether re-rating drifts (underreaction) but never asks whether that drift is already arbitraged away in the 2015-2025 half — i.e. whether the effect is available going forward.
issues.what_breaks: If the underreaction leg is real historically but decayed post-2010 (as revision-momentum broadly has), the fund sizes into a priced effect. The split-sample tests significance but not economic availability net of crowding.
issues.fix: Add a decay/availability check: compare drift magnitude 2003-2014 vs 2015-2025 explicitly, and state where this differs from standard revision-momentum (the peer-relative, within-industry framing is the plausible variant view — make that claim explicit and test it against a plain revision-momentum benchmark).

issues.summary: Type II is the expensive error here but the gates are tuned like a concentrated Type-I setting — t>5 first stage, VR>=2 stability threshold — risking discarding a real weaker effect.
issues.why_it_applies_here: This is a diversified cross-sectional L/S signal across thousands of firm-months; a false positive is absorbed across many small peer-relative bets, a missed real effect is permanent opportunity cost. A first-stage t>5 gate is far stricter than the setting's payoff warrants and could stop the project on a genuine but modest β.
issues.what_breaks: The feasibility gate could kill a tradeable effect because it demanded near-impossible significance rather than economic magnitude relevant to a diversified book.
issues.fix: Replace the t>5 kill with an economic-magnitude gate (β large enough net of turnover costs to matter over 6-18 months) plus a consistency-across-regimes gut check; reserve high t-thresholds for the single-name overlays, not the pooled first stage.

issues.summary: TAQ/tick reverse-causality check requires intraday data the fund explicitly does not have.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Context states no tick data or execution infrastructure. The identification section relies on a 'from 2010, TAQ check: pre- vs post-activation 2-hour signed returns.' The fund cannot execute this step.
issues.what_breaks: The reverse-causality control is unbuildable in-house; either it silently gets skipped (undermining the identification claim) or requires new data licensing the plan didn't budget.
issues.fix: Drop the TAQ step and substitute a daily-resolution reverse-window check (already present via CAR(-5,-2) leakage estimate), or flag the intraday check as out-of-scope and state the resulting identification limitation.

result.overall: The research design is technically strong and largely well-suited to the question — it correctly de-circularizes the multiple, uses realized LTM denominators, front-loads a feasibility kill, and states real falsifiers. But it is written for a systematic quant shop with econometric infrastructure this fundamental fund lacks, and its sophistication (Kalman β, Bai-Perron, 2SLS) cannot be defended to the PM/IC who must act on it. Strip to the inspectable core — a simple regime-bucketed β and the underreaction drift test — loosen the over-strict Type-I gates given the diversified payoff, and make the variant-view versus crowded revision-momentum explicit before this changes any position size.

result.plan_implied_asker: a quant-leaning fundamental fund with a strong data team, comfortable with panel econometrics
result.what_would_falsify: Placebo peer reassignment (500 draws) should collapse β1; ΔCAGR(t+1) should be insignificant as a pre-trend check; and if quintile-sort out-of-sample spread is flat the practical case fails.

issues.summary: The deliverable is a re-rating relationship among peers but the design measures whether the multiple moves with revisions, not whether that predicts future relative stock returns the fund would trade on.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Output is meant to change position sizing on named companies over 6-18mo. The estimator's DV is contemporaneous QoQ Δlog(EV/EBITDA) regressed on contemporaneous ΔCAGR. A contemporaneous elasticity tells you the market re-rates when consensus revises — which is largely mechanical and already priced. The tradeable question is whether a revision not yet fully reflected predicts subsequent relative return. The monthly t->t+1 version is buried as a 'timing' robustness check rather than being the headline.
issues.what_breaks: The main regression can be strongly significant and economically coherent yet carry zero investable edge, because it documents simultaneous adjustment, not anticipation. Sizing decisions built on it would be sizing on something already in the price.
issues.fix: Promote the predictive specification (revision at t, forward relative return over next 1-2 quarters) to the headline. Report the contemporaneous elasticity only as a sanity check on the pricing mechanism, not as the deliverable.

issues.summary: No stated edge relative to what is already priced — revision-multiple co-movement is among the most heavily mined relationships in equities.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan never diffs its finding against consensus or crowding. That estimate revisions drive re-ratings is textbook and traded by every quant revision/PEAD strategy. The plan's implicit edge is 'better measurement' (constant-horizon EBITDA, point-in-time Visible Alpha, EV construction with pensions/minorities), but it never establishes that this measurement improvement isolates a re-rating component that is NOT already captured by standard revision factors.
issues.what_breaks: Even a clean, significant result confirms a priced effect. Without a residualization against known revision/momentum factors, the fund cannot tell whether it has found anything incremental.
issues.fix: Add a step orthogonalizing ΔCAGR (or its predictive spread) against standard estimate-revision and price-momentum factors, and show the incremental predictive content survives. State explicitly what the market is getting wrong that this measurement captures.

issues.summary: The kill test — does anything survive out of sample and predict returns — sits at the very end behind an enormous construction and robustness apparatus.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The practical validation (out-of-sample quintile sort from 2012, spread/t-stat) is the only step that would tell the PM whether this is investable, and it is the last item. The whole point-in-time EV build, EB shrinkage, Driscoll-Kraay layering, dispersion terciles and industry interactions all precede it. A crude version — revision quintile sort on forward relative return, on the raw I/B/E/S CAGR proxy — could establish in days whether any tradeable spread exists.
issues.what_breaks: Weeks of the data team's time are committed to constructing a pristine panel before anyone has confirmed the effect predicts anything tradeable. If the cheap sort is flat, all of it was wasted.
issues.fix: Run the crude predictive quintile sort first as a gate. Only build the full point-in-time apparatus if a meaningful forward-return spread appears.

issues.summary: H1 anchors the finding to a made-up theoretical elasticity band and treats deviation from it as validation.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The '8-12%/100bp' DCF figure and the '25-50% of theoretical is coherent' rule are asserted from a two-stage/three-stage DCF with hand-picked WACC and terminal growth. This creates a self-fulfilling acceptance band: almost any β1 in a wide range will be declared 'coherent.'
issues.what_breaks: The economic validation becomes unfalsifiable — a spurious estimate landing anywhere in 25-50% of an arbitrary theoretical number gets rubber-stamped as economically sensible.
issues.fix: Drop the theoretical band as a validation gate; use it only as loose orientation. Let the placebo and out-of-sample forward-return tests carry the falsification.

issues.summary: Effort is disproportionate to a mid-size fundamental shop's ability to use and defend it.
issues.why_it_applies_here: reghdfe with 150x80 FE, two-way clustering plus Driscoll-Kraay, empirical-Bayes shrinkage, three dispersion proxies, and a full robustness grid is heavy for a fund whose output is position sizing on named companies defensible to a PM. Much of it (EB shrinkage rank stability, alternate dispersion proxies) adds researcher degrees of freedom without changing the go/no-go decision.
issues.what_breaks: The PM cannot verify the machinery, and the sheer number of specifications invites cherry-picking whichever cut looks best. The identity decomposition (β_EV=β_EBITDA+β_multiple) IS a genuinely good, checkable corroboration and should stay — but the surrounding apparatus is over-built.
issues.fix: Keep the identity decomposition and the placebo as the defensible core. Defer dispersion proxies, EB shrinkage, and half the robustness grid until the headline predictive result is established.

issues.summary: Consensus CAGR is treated as the driver, but I/B/E/S/Visible Alpha EBITDA definitions and 'consensus' are inherited premises not tested before modelling.
issues.why_it_applies_here: EBITDA definitional drift (adjusted/reported/pre-SBC) is acknowledged in pitfalls but handled by a crude |ΔCAGR|>20pp drop rule at the tail, not by verifying up front that the EBITDA the market prices matches the EBITDA in the tape. The re-rating is against whatever number investors actually use; a mismatch introduces measurement error correlated across the whole sub-industry.
issues.what_breaks: If the consensus EBITDA definition drifts systematically within an industry, the FE will not absorb it and β could reflect definitional noise rather than growth expectations.
issues.fix: Add an early diagnostic: hand-trace a sample of firm-quarters comparing the tape's EBITDA to filings and to the number in analyst notes, per key industry, before running regressions.

result.overall: The econometrics are careful and the mechanical-contamination decomposition is a genuinely good corroborating check, but the plan answers a different question than the one that pays: it measures contemporaneous re-rating (largely priced and mechanical) rather than whether revisions predict forward relative returns, and it never establishes what is incremental to standard revision/momentum factors. The single tradeable test is buried at the end behind weeks of panel construction. Reorder: run a crude predictive revision-sort as a first-week gate, residualize against known factors, and only build the pristine panel if a forward-return spread survives.

result.plan_implied_asker: single-name event-driven desk pricing one catalyst over weeks
result.what_would_falsify: Both legs must fail for a long: if full-year consensus revision is under ~0.5%, event-window CAR is under ~1 SD and under arithmetic-implied CAR, and straddle-implied move is not elevated, the checks are unpriced; then if guidance base rate and pass-through history show raises are plausible at this quarter, the long survives. Priced-in or policy-of-holding kills it.

issues.summary: Stage one gate ordering is right but the cheapest kill — management guidance policy at this fiscal quarter — is buried in stage two.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan's own default is 'no' partly because management holds the full year at this point in the calendar. If the base rate of raises at this specific fiscal quarter is near zero over 12-16 quarters, the long is dead regardless of whether checks are priced. That check is a single afternoon reading transcripts and is deterministic-ish, whereas the stage-one event study is the more elaborate work.
issues.what_breaks: You may run the full consensus-revision and event-study apparatus, gate through it, and only then discover management structurally never raises here — wasted effort on the more expensive leg.
issues.fix: Pull the guidance-history raise/hold base rate for this quarter first as a five-minute triage; if the CFO never raises at Q-whatever, write the pass note before touching the event study.

issues.summary: Arithmetic-implied CAR relies on 'defensible ACV' and 'fraction landing this fiscal year' — undisclosed inputs the desk is guessing.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The gate compares observed CAR to CAR the checks 'can arithmetically deliver,' but logo count is a non-random undersized sample (the plan admits this) and ACV/ramp-fraction are not disclosed. The implied-fundamentals anchor is therefore soft, and it drives a numeric gate threshold.
issues.what_breaks: The 'CAR under arithmetic-implied' gate condition can be pushed either way by ACV assumptions, letting the analyst rationalize into or out of the trade.
issues.fix: Report the arithmetic-implied CAR as a range under conservative/base/aggressive ACV and ramp assumptions, and require the gate to hold across the range rather than at a point estimate; treat this leg as directional, consistent with how the plan already treats the checks.

issues.summary: Regression of historical earnings-day CAR on guidance revision size has very few usable data points.
issues.why_it_applies_here: 12-16 quarters, of which only a subset had meaningful guidance revisions, is a thin regression. The plan already flags the base-rate CI as wide, but then uses a regression to 'estimate reaction' as if it produces a usable coefficient.
issues.what_breaks: The scenario-weighted expected value inherits a reaction estimate that is really eyeballing 3-4 events, and could produce false precision on sizing against the straddle.
issues.fix: Replace the regression with a simple table of the historical raise/hold events and their realized earnings-day CAR; judge by eye whether above-beat raises reliably moved the stock. Keep it as a judgeable pattern, not a fitted coefficient.

result.overall: A well-constructed single-name event-driven plan that fits the desk: it leads with the priced-in question, gates hard before spending effort on the guidance leg, states a real falsifier with both legs required, and treats the checks honestly as directional and undersized. The methods are appropriate for a two-analyst fundamental desk and the explainability supports an IC narrative. Minor improvements: triage the guidance base rate before the event study since it can kill the trade cheapest, and avoid false precision in the CAR-arithmetic anchor and the thin reaction regression.

result.plan_implied_asker: single-name event-driven desk pricing one catalyst over weeks
result.what_would_falsify: Backtest of 8 prior quarters: if positive channel commentary preceded guidance raises only 3/8 times despite 6/8 positive checks, the signal is uninformative and the plan stops. Also ~1.0x Q2 flow-through and a market-already-owns-it check.

issues.summary: The ramp/cohort least-squares fit and Monte Carlo is heavier machinery than the decision needs, and its outputs are not directly inspectable by a fundamental desk.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The gating question — does bottom-up new-logo upside clear 75bps of FY revenue — is answerable from a simple range calc (logo delta x land value x fractional in-year ramp) long before fitting R(k) by least-squares. The MC adds researcher degrees of freedom (four fitted/shocked inputs) to a two-analyst desk with no quant staff to defend it in a risk meeting.
issues.what_breaks: Methodology step: the fitted ramp and p10/50/90 can produce a false-precision number that anchors the ≥75bps gate. If the fit is overdetermined against only 12 quarters, the confidence band is illusory.
issues.fix: Run the crude bp calc first as the go/no-go screen; only build the ramp fit if the crude number lands near the 75bps threshold and the marginal precision actually changes the decision. Keep the MC as sensitivity, not as the headline output.

issues.summary: The 8-print return regression used for sizing is estimated on tiny N and treated as a mapping from estimate change to price.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Regressing 8 post-earnings returns against forward-estimate changes is 8 data points with idiosyncratic drivers each quarter; the ≥1.2x expected-vs-implied move gate rests on a slope that cannot be estimated reliably from that N.
issues.what_breaks: Position step: the ≥1.2x hurdle inherits a noisy coefficient, so the trade-selection gate is only as good as an 8-point fit that could flip on one outlier print.
issues.fix: Treat the 8 prints as a judgeable pattern (does the stock react to guide raises, and by roughly how much) rather than a fitted coefficient; state the expected move as a reasoned range anchored to realized moves, not a regression output.

issues.summary: Guidance is a management policy decision, and the plan acknowledges but does not resolve the gap between arithmetic upside and whether the CFO actually raises.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan's core deliverable is bp-of-revenue arithmetic, but the print catalyst depends on a discretionary CFO choice (tenure, macro caution, sandbagging) that the plan lists in pitfalls without a step that weights it. The 75bps arithmetic can be right and the guide still not move.
issues.what_breaks: The thesis-to-catalyst link: even if in-year sensitivity clears the bar, the print may not deliver, breaking the ≥1.5x median-raise gate for reasons the model does not capture.
issues.fix: Add an explicit read on management's guidance behavior (historical beat-and-raise cadence, CFO's stated posture, whether they typically hold beats as buffer) as a named gate alongside the arithmetic, not a footnote.

result.overall: A strong, well-fit single-name plan for this desk: it front-loads a genuine kill (the 6/8 vs 3/8 backtest stops the work in week one), separates the print catalyst from the ARR thesis, is adaptive, states real falsifiers, sizes off loss rather than an invented Sharpe, and matches Type-I-dominant burden of proof with tight, pre-committed gates. The main improvements are to run the crude bp screen before building the least-squares ramp and Monte Carlo, and to treat the 8-print return regression as a judgeable pattern rather than a fitted coefficient. Approve with those trims.

result.plan_implied_asker: a systematic quant firm with tick data, cost modelling and independent replication; horizon days-to-weeks
result.what_would_falsify: RLOIB's incremental Fama-MacBeth t<2.0 at every horizon controlling for ALLOIB/RETOIB (lot filter adds nothing); or it survives but net-of-cost long-short alpha t<3.0 (real but unharvestable).

issues.summary: The central edge question — is RLOIB incremental to the already-known subpenny/odd-lot retail signal (RETOIB) — is buried inside a full pipeline rather than run first as a cheap kill test.
issues.why_it_applies_here: RETOIB (Boehmer-Jones-Zhang-Zhang style subpenny classification) is the established, crowded retail-flow signal. The plan's entire claim to incremental value rests on RLOIB adding something over RETOIB. That residualization/rolling-window comparison could be run in days on a subsample and would answer whether the rest of the ten-year build is worth doing.
issues.what_breaks: If RLOIB is fully spanned by RETOIB the whole cost/capacity/placebo apparatus is wasted effort; the plan schedules identification alongside everything else rather than as a gate.
issues.fix: Run RLOIB-on-RETOIB residualization on 2015-2018 first as a pre-committed gate; only build the cost and capacity layers if residual RLOIB retains predictive t-stat.

issues.summary: The 't>3.0 net alpha' bar risks discarding a real but modest signal in a Type-II-dominant setting.
issues.why_it_applies_here: For a diversified quant book a missed real effect is the expensive error. A t>3.0 net-of-cost hurdle after already controlling for six factors plus in-house ALLOIB/RETOIB factors is a stiff bar; the concern is legitimate crowding here (retail-flow-fading is a well-populated trade), so a high bar is partly defensible — but the plan should state whether a t of 2.5 with good capacity would be revisited rather than binned.
issues.what_breaks: A borderline-but-tradeable diversifying sleeve could be rejected outright.
issues.fix: Pre-specify a marginal zone (e.g. 2.0<t<3.0) that triggers capacity/correlation-to-existing-book review rather than automatic rejection.

result.overall: A strong, well-sequenced plan that fits the firm exactly: it treats the round-lot retail marker as a hypothesis to validate against the known subpenny signal, front-loads a real falsifier, models costs and capacity where crowding actually kills this trade, and includes genuine placebos and negative controls. My only substantive notes are ordering — the RETOIB-spanning test is the true kill switch and should gate the expensive build — and a mild caution that the t>3.0 net bar could discard a real diversifying effect. Approve with those refinements.

result.plan_implied_asker: systematic firm with deep intraday microstructure data and a replicating research committee, days-to-weeks horizon
result.what_would_falsify: H0 explicitly stated: round lots uninformative once venue controlled; concrete kill thresholds at G1 lift<2.0x/LB<1.5x, G2 recall<35%, G3 signing<70%, G4 r<0.40, G5 |t|<3 — any single partition failing all-pass blocks Phase 2

issues.summary: Benchmark C (Rule 605 wholesaler reports) is the stated cheapest kill test but the gate structure requires all of G1-G5 to pass in one partition, and C's role in early termination is under-specified relative to its billing.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan says C is 'spreadsheet-only, run first since it alone can kill the project' but the formal gate cascade (G1-G5) is built on TAQ/RLP infrastructure. If C alone can kill, the plan should state the C-only decision rule and threshold that would stop work before any TAQ ingestion.
issues.what_breaks: Analyst may build the 36-month TAQ dataset (a quarter's work) before running the spreadsheet check that the plan itself says could kill the premise.
issues.fix: State an explicit C-only pre-screen with a numeric threshold (e.g. if wholesaler odd-lot/fractional/dollar buckets show retail has migrated off round lots below X%, stop before TAQ build).

issues.summary: G3 signing accuracy is benchmarked against RLP-flagged known-side executions, but RLP flags are the same construct feeding G1 precision — partial circularity in the validation set.
issues.why_it_applies_here: RLP-flagged executions are used both to establish precision/lift (G1) and to score signing accuracy (G3). Because RLP is near-1.0 precision but very low recall, the subset scored in G3 is a non-representative slice of retail flow, and passing G3 on it may not generalize to the round-lot population being classified.
issues.what_breaks: G3 could pass on the RLP-visible subset while signing accuracy on the broader round-lot flow (the thing actually traded) is worse, inflating confidence going into Phase 2.
issues.fix: Score signing accuracy on an independent label source (Benchmark A sub-penny) as a cross-check, and report G3 separately for RLP-visible vs. TRF-inferred flow.

issues.summary: Latent-class (Hui-Walter) estimation in G1 is sophisticated for a committee, but the plan already supplies the simple corroborating check.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Hui-Walter latent-class estimation with multiple imperfect labels is defensible here because no ground truth exists, and the plan pairs it with plain Rule 605 accounting the committee can verify by hand — this resolves the tension rather than creating one. Noting it only to confirm the corroboration is present and adequate.
issues.what_breaks: Nothing if the simple accounting agrees with the latent-class estimate; flag only if they diverge and the plan leans on the latent-class number alone.
issues.fix: Require the two G1 estimates to agree within a stated band before treating lift as established; if they diverge, default to the hand-checkable accounting figure.

result.overall: A well-constructed mechanism test that correctly refuses to bundle identification with profitability, front-loads a cheap kill (Rule 605), states an explicit H0 and pre-committed falsifiers, and matches the firm's infrastructure and Type-II-tolerant posture. The sophisticated methods are corroborated by hand-checkable simple versions, and the horizon and explainability bars fit. Minor gaps: make the Benchmark-C-only stop rule explicit so the TAQ build isn't sunk before the spreadsheet check, and remove the partial circularity of validating signing accuracy against the same RLP construct used for precision.

result.plan_implied_asker: a concentrated fundamental long-only shop deciding on one name for an IC
result.what_would_falsify: Negative on any of: negative implied gross bookings two straight quarters; channel inventory >1.5x normal; backlog/LTA definition change in a quarter that would otherwise have declined; supplier finished-goods inventory rising two quarters while backlog called record. Plus mirror-disclosure recovery <50% implies non-binding commitments.

issues.summary: The multi-episode backtest is the heaviest single work item and its usable output arrives late, yet the cheapest kill — reading this company's own agreement disclosures adversarially — could settle the question in days.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan's own thresholds (Tier 1/2 share, cash support, take-or-pay damages, RPO inclusion) are all readable directly from this company's 8-Ks, footnotes and transcripts. If the LTAs are MOUs with no cash and no take-or-pay, the thesis is dead regardless of what 2017 memory or 2000 telecom did. That check should precede assembling four historical episodes.
issues.what_breaks: Analyst time is spent reconstructing prior-cycle conversion histories before establishing whether this company's commitments have any binding quality at all; a doomed idea survives longer than it should.
issues.fix: Front-load the single-name agreement register and tiering as a gate: if this company fails the cash/take-or-pay/RPO-inclusion test, stop before the historical backtest. Use the backtest only to calibrate haircuts once the name clears the first screen.

issues.summary: Haircut percentages (90-95/70/25-35) and the calibration to the 2021-23 semi episode carry heavy weight but rest on a small number of historical episodes with idiosyncratic conversion.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Coverage math and the ≥60%/≥40% thresholds are mechanically driven by these haircuts, yet they are calibrated from a handful of prior cycles that differ in customer concentration and contract structure from this name. A one analyst IC-facing call should not hide sizing sensitivity inside a fixed haircut.
issues.what_breaks: The reverse-DCF horizon comparison and the constructive/negative verdict can flip on plausible haircut choices without the IC seeing that fragility.
issues.fix: Show the coverage conclusion under a haircut band (e.g. Tier 3 at 15% vs 35%) and state where the verdict is robust vs where it hinges on a calibration the analyst cannot defend from this company's own history.

issues.summary: RPO roll-forward solves net bookings as a plug and backs cancellations out of book-to-bill, which is a derived quantity sensitive to FX/M&A and revenue-recognition timing the disclosures may not cleanly separate.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The 'negative implied gross bookings' falsifier depends on the plug being clean. If FX, M&A, or a rev-rec change contaminates the plug, a false negative signal appears — the plan flags negative implied bookings as a kill trigger, so a measurement artifact could kill a live thesis.
issues.what_breaks: The two-quarters-negative kill criterion may fire on an accounting artifact rather than hidden cancellations.
issues.fix: Require the analyst to reconcile any negative implied-bookings quarter against explicitly disclosed FX/M&A/rev-rec items before treating it as a cancellation signal; hand-check one full roll-forward quarter end to end for the IC.
